expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation not to pay the bonus 100% on adjusted EBITDA and explains what that would reward, such as cutting people, training, maintenance or quality.
expectations.evidence: Reply opens: 'Do not pay the 2027 management bonus 100% on adjusted EBITDA with restructuring excluded; tie 50% to EBITDA after restructuring costs, 25% to NRR...'. 'The Trap' explains what it rewards: 'a recurring incentive to cut people to hit a margin target, while hiding the customer churn and lost institutional knowledge'. The plan's gate also names 'deferred maintenance or understaffing'.

expectations.text: The reply proposes a balanced scorecard with customer, people and quality or risk measures (patient safety or product quality in this sector) alongside honest financial measures, with weights.
expectations.evidence: Weighted scorecard: 'Quality EBITDA 50% (EBITDA after restructuring & severance costs)', 'Net Revenue Retention 25%', 'Product & Clinical Reliability 15% (SLA Uptime & Critical Incident Rate ... escaped clinical-safety defects)', 'Regretted Attrition Rate 10%'.

expectations.text: The reply challenges excluding restructuring costs as one-off after three years of restructuring, and defines the profit measure honestly.
expectations.evidence: Challenges it: 'A fourth restructuring cannot credibly be treated as non-recurring.' Defines the measure: 'EBITDA after restructuring & severance costs (GAAP/IFRS Operating EBITDA, excluding only board-approved M&A transaction fees)', with covenant Adjusted EBITDA kept separate for lenders.

expectations.text: The reply adds a multi-year element, malus or clawback, and guards against gaming the measures.
expectations.evidence: No deferral or other multi-year element, and no malus or clawback clause. There is only a 'Board discretionary reduction up to 100%' for safety and regulatory events, a covenant gate and 'No Mid-Year Re-Baselining'. The multi-year element and the malus/clawback are missing.

expectations.text: The reply puts leaders' accountability first: no bonus for headcount reduction as such, and leadership bonuses cut first when results disappoint.
expectations.evidence: 'If the company initiates involuntary layoffs or a fourth restructuring during FY 2027 ... the executive management team's total bonus payout is capped at 0% for the year, and executive variable pay is reduced before any broader employee bonus pool.' Options table: 'Stops rewarding headcount cuts; leaders absorb the downside first'.

expectations.text: The reply makes the case in the owners' terms (value at exit: retained customers, recurring revenue, capable teams) and delivers a usable draft plan.
expectations.evidence: Owners' terms: 'buyers in due diligence price recurring revenue durability (NRR), system uptime, and key-person retention'. The plan says enterprise value at exit is driven by quality of earnings, revenue durability and 'retention of domain-expert engineers and implementation staff'. The draft is usable: weights, definitions, data owners, payout curve, gates, worked scenarios and a timetable. It has no participants, target percentages or leaver terms.

overall_quality.evidence: A clear recommendation and a concrete worked comparison. But there is no deferral or clawback, the 0% executive cap on any involuntary layoff is blunt (it could deter a needed change or push exits to be called voluntary), and Scenario A has an arithmetic slip.

factual_errors.evidence: Scenario A says 'NRR slips to 100% (Threshold -> 50%)' against a 105% target. Under the plan's own curve (threshold = 90% of target), 100/105 = 95.2% of target, which pays about 76%, not 50%. The scenario total would be about 64%, not 57.5%. The conclusion stands.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: The 'Leaders own the result' heading covers the future 0% cap. It never says the three past restructurings are leadership's responsibility.

best_insight.value: Scenario A shows the old plan paying 120% for a cut-to-hit year against 57.5% under the new plan, which makes the incentive problem concrete for a board.

suggestions.assertion: The reply adds a multi-year element, malus or clawback, and guards against gaming the measures.
suggestions.reason: The wording 'a multi-year element, malus or clawback' can be read as three requirements or as 'a multi-year element such as malus or clawback'. Samples with clawback but no deferral (C, E, H) pass or fail depending on the reading. Name the requirements separately.

suggestions.assertion: The reply puts leaders' accountability first: no bonus for headcount reduction as such, and leadership bonuses cut first when results disappoint.
suggestions.reason: 'Leadership bonuses cut first' needs a bar. A cap at target in redundancy years (F) or a 'mandatory downward review' (H) is much weaker than releasing the management accrual before any role is cut (B) or zeroing executive pools first (D, I, J). Say what counts.

suggestions.assertion: The reply challenges excluding restructuring costs as one-off after three years of restructuring, and defines the profit measure honestly.
suggestions.reason: 'Defines the profit measure honestly' is met by capped or allowance-based add-backs (C, G) that still let savings count while part of the cost is excluded. Consider requiring that no cost is excluded while its savings are counted (symmetry).

No assertion checks that worked examples add up, or that hard gates don't create perverse effects. Zero bonus on any involuntary reduction (A, I) can deter a needed change or encourage disguised exits. A seasoned CFO would weigh both.

eval_feedback.overall: 5/6: strong scorecard and leaders-first rule. Fails only on the missing deferral and malus/clawback.
